title: Infra engineering playbook: GPU fleet, capacity, Terraform/IaC modules, CI/CD and runbooks
author: Asha Patel
content:
Overview

This playbook consolidates the infrastructure engineering standards and operational procedures for Redwood's GPU fleet and associated infra: capacity planning, cloud accounts and networking, Terraform / IaC modules, CI/CD pipelines and runbooks. It is intended for infra engineers, SREs, platform owners, and on-call responders.

Scope

- GPU fleet topology and node types (hosted/dedicated/private).
- Capacity planning cadence and forecasting.
- Cloud accounts, VPC/network design, peering, and ACLs.
- Terraform modules and IaC patterns used by the infra team.
- CI/CD pipeline definitions, test strategies, and promotion workflows.
- Runbooks for common GPU-related incidents and day-2 operations.

Ownership & Routines

- Primary owner: infra/gpu-fleet (team lead: @Diego Morales).
- Secondary owners: infra-networking, infra-ci-cd, eng-sre.
- Weekly cadence: capacity review (Wednesdays 10:00 PT).
- Quarterly: forecast review aligned with product roadmap.

GPU Fleet architecture (high-level)

- Fleet regions: us-west-2 (primary), eu-west-1 (secondary), ap-northeast-1 (staging/partner).
- Node classes: compute-gpu-rtx (inference-optimized, 8xA100), compute-gpu-ml (training-sparing, mixed GPU fleet), burst-gpu (spot-backed for non-critical workloads).
- Scheduler: internal serving-runtime scheduler + autoscaler for stateless inference workers.
- Storage: remote checkpoint store (S3-compatible) + local NVMe for model caching.

Capacity planning

Goals and SLOs
1. 99th percentile p90 token latency SLO per model-route: target 200ms for common routes, 500ms for long-context workloads.
2. Throughput headroom: maintain 25% spare capacity on peak expected load.
3. Availability SLO: 99.9% fleet-wide for Dedicated pools.

Key metrics to monitor (collected in dashboards)
- GPU utilization (per-node, per-pool) - target: steady-state 55-75%.
- Queue depth and request wait time.
- Pod restart rate / OOM/eviction counts.
- Cold-start frequency (cache misses).
- Spot preemption rate (for spot-backed pools).

Forecasting process
1. Collect 90/95/99 percentile traffic projections from product and growth team.
2. Map traffic to tokens/sec per model and translate to GPU-hours using benchmarked tokens/sec per node.
3. Apply safety buffer: +25% for headroom and +15% for region failover.
4. Run procurement or cloud capacity reservation process 30-60 days before expected peak.

Thresholds and alerts
- GPU utilization >80% sustained for 10m -> page infra-oncall (P1 prep).
- Queue wait time >200ms for p95 -> page infra-oncall.
- Pod OOM rate >5% of pool in 15m -> page SRE.

Cloud accounts and networking

Account topology and security boundaries
- Per-environment accounts: prod, staging, integration, sandbox.
- Dedicated customer deployments use VPC-isolated accounts and cross-account roles.
- Shared services account for logging, monitoring, and artifact registry.

VPC & subnet design
- Each region: 3 AZs, public subnets for load balancers, private subnets for GPU nodes + NAT gateways as required.
- CIDR plan: /16 per account, split into /20 per AZ.
- Security groups: minimal egress/ingress, enforce mTLS between runtime services.

Network connectivity patterns
- Private link and VPC peering for critical control-plane traffic.
- Transit gateway used for multi-account connectivity in prod.
- Egress policies: restrict outbound to necessary artifact registries and model stores.

IAM and secrets
- Principle of least privilege for cross-account roles.
- Short-lived assume-role flows for runtime agents.
- KMS-backed keys for model encryption; HSM for regulatory customers (Private).

Terraform / IaC modules and patterns

Module registry and ownership
- Registry: internal module registry (terraform-modules.redwood.internal).
- Maintainers: infra-iac team.
- Module types: networking, gpu-pool, autoscaler, iam-role, monitoring, efs/nvme-storage, dns & loadbalancer.

Patterns and guidelines
- Small modules: each module should do one thing and have a clear, documented interface. Avoid monolith modules that cross domains.
- Inputs/outputs: use clear variable naming, avoid sensitive outputs.
- Versioning: use semantic versioning for modules; pin module versions in root workspaces.
- State management: remote state per environment using encrypted backend (S3 + DynamoDB locking).

Example module usage (snippet)
- This is a representative example (abbreviated):

terraform {
  backend "s3" {
    bucket = "redwood-terraform-state-prod"
    key    = "gpu-pool/us-west-2/terraform.tfstate"
    region = "us-west-2"
  }
}

module "gpu_pool_a100" {
  source          = "git::ssh://git@github.com/redwood/terraform-modules.git//gpu-pool?ref=v1.2.0"
  name            = "a100-inference-pool"
  node_type       = "a100-80gb"
  desired_count   = 10
  min_count       = 2
  max_count       = 20
  network_subnet  = module.vpc.private_subnet_ids
}

CI/CD and build pipeline standards

Pipeline goals
- Fast feedback for infra changes (lint -> plan -> test -> apply).
- Safe promotion to prod via staged workspaces and manual approvals for critical changes.
- Automated acceptance tests for Terraform modules and integration smoke tests.

Pipeline stages (recommended)
1. Pre-commit checks: terraform fmt, tflint, static checks.
2. Plan stage: terraform plan in ephemeral workspace; post plan as PR comment with plan image diff.
3. Unit tests: mock provider/unit tests (terratest).
4. Integration tests: deploy to sandbox/integration account and run basic smoke tests (node boot, scheduler registration, simple inference).
5. Approval gate: owners approve production promotion (manual).
6. Apply to prod: run apply in production workspace with state locking and audit logs.

Pipeline implementation notes
- CI runner: self-hosted runners for secrets access during integration tests.
- Use ephemeral AWS creds from CI via OIDC where possible; rotate long-lived keys.
- Keep apply runs under a restricted service account and record who triggered applies.

Testing matrix
- Unit tests for all modules.
- Integration smoke test: deploy gpu-pool=1 node + attach model-cache -> run 100 inference requests.
- Canary rollout test: validate autoscaler trigger under synthetic load.

Runbooks and on-call playbooks

1) GPU node OOM / eviction
- Symptoms: increased pod restarts, kubelet evictions, elevated OOM counts.
- Immediate steps:
  1. Check affected node(s): kubectl describe node <node> and kubectl top pod -n serving.
  2. Confirm whether OOM is due to pod memory or GPU memory exhaustion (check container logs + dmesg).
  3. If node unstable: cordon node, drain with --ignore-daemonsets, restart node agent, and allow autoscaler to replace.
  4. If caused by model size/config: rollback recent model rollout or reduce max_batch_size.
  5. Post-incident: create infra ticket with root-cause and size-adjusted baseline.

2) Autoscaler failing to scale up
- Symptoms: queue depth increasing, utilization below expected because new pods are pending.
- Immediate steps:
  1. Inspect ClusterAutoscaler logs and controller-manager.
  2. Validate IAM permissions for node-launch role.
  3. Check capacity reservations and spot availability in cloud provider.
  4. Temporarily increase desired_count or use burst-gpu pool.

3) Networking failure between control-plane and GPU nodes
- Symptoms: nodes register/deregister frequently, RPC timeouts to control-plane.
- Immediate steps:
  1. Check VPC route tables and transit gateway health.
  2. Verify security group rules and NACLs.
  3. If cross-account role changes were applied recently, roll back or re-apply correct trust policy.

Upgrade and rollback playbook

Planned upgrade (e.g., kernel, driver, runtime)
1. Create upgrade RFC/PR with exact change set and testing plan.
2. Validate in integration account: node bootstrap, driver install, run smoke tests.
3. Canary in prod: upgrade 1 AZ or 10% of nodes, monitor key signals for 60-120 minutes.
4. If stable, proceed with rolling upgrade across remaining nodes per-AZ.
5. If regression detected: run rollback steps and open postmortem.

Rollback steps (critical)
- Restore previous machine image or driver version from AMI snapshots.
- Recreate node pool with pinned older launch template and migrate workloads.

Day-2 operations checklist
- Daily: check critical dashboards (GPU utilization, queue depth, node health).
- Weekly: run small-scale synthetic load test and validate autoscaler triggers.
- Monthly: capacity forecast meeting and spend review (GPU-hour & spot loss).

Troubleshooting cheat-sheet (commands)
- k get nodes -o wide
- kubectl describe pod <pod> -n serving
- kubectl logs <pod> -n serving --previous
- aws ec2 describe-instances --filters "Name=tag:Name,Values=redwood-gpu*"
- terraform plan -var-file=env/prod.tfvars

Post-incident and RCA expectations
- Every P1/P0 incident must have a postmortem within 72 hours with action items assigned.
- Include timeline, detection, mitigation steps, root cause, and preventive measures (e.g., better autoscaling thresholds, pre-warming cache).

Appendix: example CI job YAML (abbreviated)

- job: terraform-plan
  stage: plan
  script:
    - terraform init -backend-config="bucket=redwood-terraform-state-prod"
    - terraform fmt -check
    - terraform validate
    - terraform plan -out=plan.tfplan
  artifacts:
    paths: [plan.tfplan]

Contacts and escalation
- Primary on-call: infra-oncall (rotate) -> page: #infra-oncall.
- Pager escalation: infra-sre -> eng-sre lead (Chen Li).
- Module ownership: infra-iac owners (see module registry).
